summary: Specifies the Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS), a protocol that helps iSNS clients and servers discover, manage and configure iSCSI and Fibre Channel devices on an IP network. It provides discovery services comparable to those in Fibre Channel networks. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A school directory tells you where each class is. iSNS is a directory for storage devices on a network, so computers can find the disks they need.

questions: how do iscsi devices discover each other
what is an isns discovery domain
subtitle: A directory service that lets storage devices on an IP network find each other and be managed from one place.

tldr.problem: Storage devices on an IP network were configured one by one, each with its own list of known initiators and targets. That does not scale as the number of devices grows.
tldr.mechanism: iSNS adds a server that holds a database of registered devices. Clients register themselves, query for peers, are grouped into discovery domains and receive state change notifications, all over a binary protocol carried on TCP or UDP.
tldr.outcome: iSNS gives an IP network discovery and management services comparable to those in Fibre Channel networks. Its use is optional for iSCSI and required for iFCP.

today: RFC 4171 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is part of a set with RFC 3720 (iSCSI) and RFC 4172 (iFCP).

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4171 specifies the Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS) protocol, which iSCSI and iFCP devices use to talk to an iSNS server. iSCSI is SCSI encapsulated for TCP/IP, and iFCP is a gateway-to-gateway protocol that connects Fibre Channel and SCSI devices over TCP/IP.

Without iSNS, each storage device is configured by hand with its own list of known initiators and targets. With iSNS, every device hands its discovery and management work to the server, which becomes the single configuration point for a management station. The document focuses on the exchange between iSNS servers and clients. Interactions among several authoritative primary servers are left as a possible topic for future work.

Use of iSNS is OPTIONAL for iSCSI and REQUIRED for iFCP. All frame formats are in big endian network byte order.
sections.eli5: Instead of every kid keeping their own list of where everyone sits, the school keeps one big seating chart that everybody can ask.

sections.title: Components and the Four Services
sections.content:
An iSNS client runs inside a storage device. It can register the device's attributes, download information about other clients in a shared discovery domain and receive notifications. A management station is a special client with access to all discovery domains. The iSNS server answers queries, stores properly authenticated registrations in its database and sends notifications. The database can be kept in an LDAP directory.

The server provides four main functions:

  • Name registration: targets and initiators register in the database and query for others. It is modeled on the Fibre Channel Generic Services Name Server.
  • Discovery Domain and Login Control: devices must share at least one enabled discovery domain to learn about each other, and targets can delegate their list of authorized initiators to the server.
  • State Change Notification (SCN): the server tells clients about changes to the database. Regular SCNs are limited to the domains where the event happened, while management SCNs are only for Control Nodes.
  • Open mapping: the database can hold the mapping between Fibre Channel devices and iSCSI devices, so any authorized client can read it instead of it being locked inside a gateway.
sections.eli5: The directory does four jobs: it lists everyone, decides who may see whom, sends a message when something changes, and knows how two different kinds of devices match up.

sections.title: The iSNS Object Model
sections.content:
The database stores a small set of object types. A Network Entity is a container for Storage Nodes and Portals, and no object can be in more than one Network Entity. A Portal is an interface identified by an IP address and a TCP/UDP port. A Storage Node is the logical endpoint of an iSCSI or iFCP session, identified by its iSCSI Name or, for iFCP, its FC Port Name (WWPN).

A Portal Group ties a Portal to an iSCSI Node. A Portal reaches a node only if the Portal Group Tag (PGT) is non-NULL. Portals sharing the same PGT for a node give coordinated access, meaning a single iSCSI session can span them. An FC Device represents a Fibre Channel node and is identified by its WWNN.

A Discovery Domain (DD) is a container for Storage Nodes and Portals. A non-Control-Node client only sees objects with which it shares at least one active DD. A Discovery Domain Set (DDS) groups DDs, and a DD is active if it belongs to at least one active DDS.
sections.eli5: Think of a building (the entity) with doors (portals) and rooms (storage nodes). Clubs (discovery domains) decide which rooms can see each other.

sections.title: The iSNSP Message Format
sections.content:
Every iSNSP PDU starts with a 12-byte header: iSNSP VERSION, FUNCTION ID, PDU LENGTH, FLAGS, TRANSACTION ID and SEQUENCE ID, each 16 bits. The version in this document is 0x0001. A function ID with the leading bit set is a response. The payload length must be 4-byte aligned.

The FLAGS field marks whether the sender is the client or server, whether an authentication block is present, the replace flag for DevAttrReg, and the first and last PDU of a message. One message can span several PDUs. The first uses sequence ID 0 and later ones count up, and the two-byte field allows up to 65536 PDUs per message. A reply reuses the request's transaction ID.

The payload carries attributes in a Tag-Length-Value layout: a 4-byte tag, a 4-byte length and then the value. Values are padded with zero bytes to a 4-byte boundary. Responses begin with a 4-byte status code where 0 means success and a non-zero code rejects the whole request. Codes run from 0 up to 23.

Multicast and broadcast messages, which means the heartbeat, can carry an authentication block with a timestamp and a signature. Unicast messages SHOULD NOT include it and should rely on IPsec.
sections.eli5: Each message has an envelope with a label saying what it is, how long it is and which conversation it belongs to. Inside are little notes, each saying what it is about and how big it is.

sections.title: Finding Servers, Backups and Transport
sections.content:
Clients can find an iSNS server in three ways: the Service Location Protocol (SLP), a DHCP option, or the iSNS heartbeat message. The heartbeat is the only iSNS message sent by multicast or broadcast. It is sent by the active server and tells listeners the address of the active server and of any backup servers, a heartbeat interval and a counter.

Query and registration messages run over TCP or UDP, and the server MUST accept TCP connections for client registrations. With UDP, each datagram MUST contain exactly one iSNS PDU. The server opens the connections used to deliver ESI and SCN messages to the client.

Backup servers keep a copy of the primary's database. A backup that loses connectivity to the active server and to backups of higher precedence SHOULD assume the active role. Clients do not need to re-register when this happens. The document does not specify the full protocol between servers for stable failover. Records can also move between servers by other means such as LDAP or SNMP.
sections.eli5: Kids can find the directory by asking around, by a note on the door, or by hearing the teacher's regular announcement. If the teacher is out, the substitute takes over without anyone starting over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists three threats: an attacker could alter messages to point devices at rogue peers, could pose as the server with false heartbeats, or could learn about devices by snooping. Unicast messages may need authentication, and confidentiality is desirable and REQUIRED for some server functions.

Clients MUST be able to authenticate multicast or broadcast messages using the iSNS authentication block, which has the same format as the SLP block, and MUST support BSD value 0x002. For unicast messages, servers that support security MUST implement ESP in tunnel mode, and implementations MUST support IKE Main Mode and Aggressive Mode. Manual keying SHOULD NOT be used. If the server distributes security policy, authentication, integrity and confidentiality MUST be used. DES SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: A fake announcer could send everyone to the wrong place, so real announcements are signed, and private conversations are locked in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The well-known TCP and UDP port for iSNS is 3205. The RFC creates two IANA registries: one of block storage protocols supported by iSNS, and one of standard iSNS attributes. New attributes need IETF Consensus, and the RFC that adds one must give its tag value, length and permissible keys. The Block Structure Descriptor registry for the authentication block is the one from RFC 2608.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of numbers for the directory's door and its kinds of notes, and new entries must be approved.

fields.name: Function ID
fields.desc: Message type; the leading bit set means a response.

fields.name: PDU Length
fields.desc: Length of the payload in bytes, 4-byte aligned.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Sender type, authentication block, replace, last and first PDU.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Unique per outstanding request; replies reuse it.

fields.name: Sequence ID
fields.desc: Starts at zero for the first PDU of a message.
